text.p: These are the main stories in Latvian newspapers on Tuesday. Prepared for Reuters by the Co-operation Fund. Reuters has not verified these reports and does not vouch for their accuracy:
- The three largest parties in the ruling coalition -- Latvia's Way, For Fatherland and Freedom and Saimnieks -- voiced their formal support to the cabinet of Guntars Krasts.

- Parties are to finalise talks on the new government declaration, expected to be little different from the previous government programme with a balanced budget and inflation planned at nine percent this year and seven percent next year.

- Left-wing Social Democrat leader Juris Bojars announced that his party will bring a suit against Lattelekom in late August or early September. He alleges that the company is cheating its clients by charging them for analogue local calls without improving the quality.
- Prime minister candidate Guntar Krasts sets out his aims in an interview with the newspaper.
- The leader of the Party of National Reforms, Alexander Kirshteins, predicts the new government will not survive until the next parliamentary election due in October 1998.
- Sweden has become the fifth Nordic country to sign a visa-free agreement with Latvia.
- Einars Tupuritis was third in the 800 metre preliminary heats at the World Championships in Athens

- Efraim Zhuroff, the director of the Simon Wiesenthal Institute in Israel, believes that a Swiss bank account owned by former Latvian president Albert Kviesis may have been used by the Nazis as Kviesis collaborated with the German administration in Latvia in 1942-1943.

- The director general of the Latvian Privatisation Agency, Janis Naglis said the agency does not plan to make state-owned VEF insolvent until at least one of its daughter companies finds investments, possibly from Hitachi.
